reason: E1 and E2 support that high-entropy oxides improve CO oxidation activity and stability, and that Pt on HEO resists sintering and hydrothermal deactivation. However, neither passage provides evidence for the key premise that a thermal post-treatment of a near-equiatomic alloy catalyst will form a nanoporous high-entropy oxide surface layer, nor that such a layer resists NO poisoning or enables light-off below 150 °C. The cited evidence is thus only partly relevant to the proposed intervention and mechanism.
premises: Increasing configurational disorder in spinel oxides lowers CO oxidation T10 and improves stability (E1).
Pt nanoparticles on high-entropy oxide (HEO) show exceptional thermal stability and sinter-resistance during CO oxidation (E2).
Pt/HEO retains activity and porous structure under hydrothermal cycling with minimal Pt particle growth (E2).
A thermal post-treatment in oxidizing, humid atmosphere can form a nanoporous high-entropy oxide surface layer on a multi-principal-element alloy.
The high-entropy oxide layer stabilizes PGM sites, suppresses sintering, and resists poisoning by H2O and NO.
